content_voiceover: This slide breaks down the causes of secondary hemostasis disorders, meaning problems within the coagulation cascade itself rather than platelets. The congenital group covers inherited single-factor deficiencies. Hemophilia A comes from a deficiency of factor eight, and hemophilia B, also called Christmas disease, comes from a deficiency of factor nine. Both are X-linked recessive, so they mainly affect males, though carrier females can occasionally bleed. Other rarer congenital deficiencies, like factor eleven deficiency, also fall into this category. The second branch is acquired hemophilia, which is completely different biology. It's not inherited. It results from autoantibodies that develop against a clotting factor, usually factor eight, in someone with no prior bleeding history. This typically shows up in older adults and is linked to autoimmune disease, malignancy, or the postpartum period, and it needs a very different diagnostic workup than the congenital forms.
keypoints: Hemophilia A is caused by factor VIII deficiency, X-linked recessive
Hemophilia B, or Christmas disease, is caused by factor IX deficiency, X-linked recessive
Other rare congenital factor deficiencies also exist
Acquired hemophilia involves autoantibodies against a factor, usually FVIII, and is not inherited
keypoint_voiceover: To summarize, hemophilia A is factor eight deficiency, hemophilia B is factor nine deficiency, both X-linked, and both are congenital. Acquired hemophilia is a completely different entity, driven by autoantibodies rather than genetics, and it shows up later in life without any family history.
